newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: IMF cautions Bangladesh against wage rises.
newsitem.headline: IMF cautions Bangladesh against wage rises.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund (IMF), which is urging Bangladesh to cut expenditure to shore up its sagging economy, has said the government should not award major pay rises to state employees.
"Preliminary indications pointed to substantial overruns on current expenditure, including the wage bill," said an IMF report obtained by Reuters on Saturday.
The government spends $990 million a year on wages for state employees and it was not immediately clear what increase Dhaka was contemplating.
The report suggested the government of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina exercise caution in financial matters.
"Any wage increases proposed by the National Pay Commission should not be applied retroactively to 1996/97," it said.
Hasina formed the commission to review the pay scales for government employees after she assumed power last June. It is assumed new pay scales might go into effect in July this year.
The government is under pressure from employees to make new wages effective from the start of the current financial year, which started in July last year.
The report noted the new government's belief that restoration of macro-economic stability was a prerequisite for creating an environment conducive to higher investment and rapid sustainable growth.

"For 1996/97, the government aimed to raise the rate of growth of GDP to 5.5 percent, reduce the rate of inflation to less than 5 percent and build up external (foreign exchange) reserves to $2.3 billion.
"Progress in the above areas has been mixed so far in 1996/97. The recovery of industrial activity, investment and exports has been slower than expected," the report said.
"In the external finances, the current account deficit narrowed markedly during the first five months of the fiscal year despite the lacklustre performance of exports.
"This reflected subdued imports, due mainly to the bumper rice crop and sluggish domestic and external demand. In addition, workers' remittances (from abroad) increased sharply."
Bangladesh consumer prices rose 0.23 percent in December, giving a year-on-year rise of 4.05 percent, according to government figures released on Friday.

The report said that with the outlook for exports remaining weak, any strengthening in domestic demand and a rise in imports could quickly lead to a widening of the balance of payments deficit. This would likely cause a further decline in reserves from an already low level.
The current account deficit was $1.27 billion in 1995/96 against $1.03 billion the previous year. The reserves stood at $1.86 billion at the end of January, central bank sources said.
The IMF, however, praised the current year budget, saying it had "envisaged raising government revenue by 17 percent, strictly limiting the growth of current expenditure...
"Accordingly, fiscal policy aims at keeping the budget deficit within prudent limits, so as to meet essential public investment needs without straining available resources.
